case_title: Almeida v. Ceylon Fisheries Corporation and Others (1998)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the refusal of the Ceylon Fisheries Corporation to grant the petitioner a one-year extension of service after he reached the optional retirement age of 55 amounted to arbitrary or discriminatory treatment in violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, Marketing Manager of the Ceylon Fisheries Corporation, claimed that he had a long and unblemished service record and a legitimate expectation of receiving an extension of service for one year beyond the optional retirement age of 55. He argued that the Board’s refusal was discriminatory and capricious because he had previously been exonerated in a disciplinary inquiry and had even been promoted to a special grade executive post in 1996 despite the pending magistrate’s court case. He contended that several other employees had been given extensions, and therefore the refusal to extend his service violated Articles 12(1) and 12(2).
respondent_argument: The respondents submitted that the Board of Directors possessed full discretion to grant or refuse extensions of service after an employee reached the optional retirement age. At its 725th meeting on 2 September 1996, the Board had formally decided that extensions would only be granted to employees with a satisfactory record and whose services were indispensable. The petitioner was denied an extension because there was a pending criminal prosecution against him relating to forgery, and because his services were not considered indispensable. The respondents also clarified that some employees cited by the petitioner had received extensions before the policy change, while the rest received extensions only because they met the indispensability requirement.
interpretation_summary: The Court examined the petitioner’s letter of appointment and subsequent promotions, noting that none of the documents guaranteed employment beyond the age of 55. The governing administrative circulars and Board decisions clearly established that extension beyond the optional retirement age was not a right but a matter entirely within the discretion of the appointing authority. The Board had adopted a formal policy (4R1) requiring that extensions be granted only to employees who had a good past record and whose services were indispensable. The Court held that discretionary powers may be exercised so long as they are based on relevant considerations and are not arbitrary or irrational. The Board had considered the petitioner’s application and relied on two legitimate factors: (1) a pending criminal prosecution against him, and (2) the determination that his services were not indispensable. These were valid administrative considerations. The Court further noted that the petitioner failed to prove unequal treatment, as the examples he cited were either employees who obtained extensions before the new policy or employees who met the indispensability requirement. Thus, the refusal to extend the petitioner’s service was neither arbitrary nor discriminatory.
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the application. It held that the refusal to grant the petitioner an extension of service was based on valid considerations and did not amount to arbitrary or capricious administrative action under Article 12(1). The petitioner was not entitled to relief, and the application was dismissed without costs.
principles_established: Extension of service beyond the optional retirement age is not a right; it is a matter of discretion.
Administrative discretion must be exercised based on relevant considerations but is not unconstitutional merely because it disadvantages a particular applicant.
Refusal to grant discretionary benefits such as service extensions does not violate Article 12(1) unless the decision is arbitrary, irrational, capricious, or discriminatory.
A pending criminal prosecution is a valid consideration when deciding whether to extend an employee’s service.
Comparative claims of discrimination must show that other employees who were similarly situated received favourable treatment; mere difference in outcome is insufficient.
full_text:
ALMEIDA v. CEYLON FISHERIES CORPORATION AND OTHERS
SUPREME COURT
DHEERARATNE, J., ANANDACOOMARASWAMY, J. AND GUNASEKERA, J.
S.C. APPLICATION NO. 310/97 (FR)
MAY 13, 1998.
Fundamental rights - Refusal to grant an extension of service - Discretion of the appointing authority - Art. 12 (1) of the Constitution.
The petitioner was the Marketing Manager of the 1st respondent corporation. On reaching the age of 55 years which was the age of optional retirement, he applied for an extension of service for one year. The petitioner's application was rejected by the Board of Directors of the 1st respondent corporation having regard to the fact that there was a criminal prosecution pending against the petitioner and that his service was not indispensable.
Held:
There was a discretion vested in the Board of the 1st respondent corporation to grant or refuse an extension of service after an officer reached the optional age of retirement. The decision of the Board to refuse an extension of service to the petitioner could not be said to be arbitrary or capricious and violative of Article 12 of the Constitution.
APPLICATION for relief for infringement of fundamental rights.
Upul Jayasuriya with P. Radhakrishnan for petitioner.
Shavindra Fernando SSC for Attorney-General.
Cur. adv. vult.
June 8, 1998.
GUNASEKERA, J.
The petitioner who was the Marketing Manager of the 1st respondent Corporation complains of the violation of his fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 12 (1) and 12 (2) of the Constitution by the Corporation's refusal to grant him an extension of service for one year from 1.1.97 on his reaching the age of 55 years.
The petitioner had been appointed to the post of Marketing Officer in Grade IX of the Fisheries Corporation with effect from 26.7.1965 by a letter of appointment marked 'P1'. Over the years he had been promoted to higher grades and had been appointed to the post of Marketing Manager, Grade I, with effect from 1.11.1986 by a letter of appointment 'P3' dated 11.11.1986 and thereafter had been promoted to a special grade executive post with effect from 1.1.1996 by letter 'P4'.
It is to be noted that none of the letters 'P1', 'P3' & 'P4' specify an age of retirement but however, 'P4' & 'P3' refer to the terms and conditions specified in the original letter of appointment 'P1'. Clause 2 of 'P1' issued to the petitioner inter alia states: "you will be subjected to the administrative, financial and disciplinary Orders of the Corporation and any other Orders issued from time to time by or on behalf of the Board" and Clause 16 states: "after you are confirmed in your appointment your employment is terminable on the giving of three months' written notice or on the appointment of three months' salary in lieu thereof on either side".
By a notice dated 19.3.1996 marked 'P5' the 4th respondent had notified all Staff Officers who intended to continue in service in the 1st respondent Corporation after attaining 55 years of age to forward a request indicating their desire to continue in service 6 months prior to reaching 55 years. Since the petitioner would have reached 55 years of age on 1.1.97 he had by letter 'P6' dated 2.6.96 requested that he be granted an extension of service for one year from 1.1.97. The petitioner had been informed by the 4th respondent by 'P7' dated 14.11.96 that his application for an extension of service after 55 years was rejected consequent upon a policy decision taken by the Board of Directors of the 1st respondent Corporation and that steps would be taken to treat him as being retired from 1.1.97. The petitioner states that subsequently by an internal circular No. 97-01 dated 15.1.97 marked 'P9' that the Common Policy Decision of the Board of Directors of the 1st respondent Corporation not to engage employees whomsoever beyond the age of 55 years was amended to fall in line with a Secretarial Division Circular No. SEC 131/1 dated 26.10.65 marked 'P8' according to which the Board had decided that the age of retirement of employees of the 1st respondent Corporation should be (1) 55 years for optional retirement and (2) 60 years for compulsory retirement.
It was contended for and on behalf of the petitioner that Circular 'P9' further provided that those employees who had been retired on reaching the age of 55 years between December, 1996 and January, 1997 could make an application for an extension of service for the consideration by the Board, and in consequence of that provision that the petitioner applied for an extension of service for one year by his letter dated 16.1.1997 marked 'P10' and that his request for an extension of service was rejected by the 2nd respondent by letter dated 24.2.97 marked 'P2'.
It was urged by learned counsel for the petitioner that the rejection of the application of the petitioner for an extension of service by one year from 1.1.97 was violative of the provisions of Articles 12 (1) and 12 (2) of the Constitution since the rejection was capricious and discriminatory. It was submitted on behalf of the petitioner that during his long period of service of over 30 years that he had not been found wanting in respect of any aspect of his work and had a reasonable expectation of securing an extension of service after reaching the age of 55. Further it was contended that the petitioner had been exonerated by the Inquiring Officer who had held a disciplinary inquiry in 1991 and notwithstanding the fact that the petitioner had a case No. B 274/94 in the Magistrate's Court of Anuradhapura which never got off the ground that he was promoted to a special grade executive post with effect from 1.1.96.
Learned Senior State Counsel appearing for the respondents submitted that the Board at its 725th Board Meeting held on 2.9.96 considered the question of granting extension of service to its employees who had reached the optional age of retirement (55 years) and decided that extension of service beyond the optional age of retirement would be considered only in the case of employees who had a satisfactory past record of service and whose services were indispensable. A copy of the said Board decision had been filed along with the affidavit of the 4th respondent marked '4R1'. In the case of the petitioner it was submitted that the Board had considered his application for an extension of service after 55 years and refused to accede to his request since a criminal prosecution relating to forgery was pending in the Magistrate's Court and that his services were not indispensable. A copy of the said Board decision dated 18.2.97 had been produced marked 'X' along with a further affidavit of the 4th respondent dated 28.10.97.
Although the petitioner has referred to several persons whose services have been extended after reaching the optional age of retirement in paragraph 25 of the petition the respondent's position is that two of them, namely Titus and Weeraratne, had been granted extensions of service prior to the Board decision '4R1' and Nandasiri Gunaratne and Podi Appuhamy had not been granted extensions as averred by the petitioner. That the others have been granted extensions of service on the basis that their services were indispensable in accordance with the circular '4R1'.
On a consideration of the documents filed it appears that there is a discretion vested in the Board of the 1st respondent Corporation to grant or to refuse an extension of service after an officer reaches the optional age of retirement. The discretion is to be exercised within the framework of the principles laid down in the Board decision marked '4R1'. In the instant case after a consideration of the application for the extension of the services of the petitioner the Board having had regard to the fact that there was a criminal prosecution pending against the petitioner and on account of the fact that his services were not indispensable has refused to exercise the discretion in his favour and intimated the said decision by letter marked 'P2' dated 24.2.97. The said decision, in my view, cannot be said to be arbitrary or capricious. Accordingly, the petitioner's application is dismissed without costs.
DHEERARATNE, J. - I agree.
ANANDACOOMARASWAMY, J. - I agree.
Application dismissed.
source: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 310/97 (FR), decided on 8 June 1998

case_title: Amerasinghe v. Board of Directors, Co-operative Wholesale Establishment (1998)
judges: G. P. S. De Silva C.J.

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether refusing the petitioner’s second extension of service based on adverse committee reports—without giving him any opportunity to respond—was arbitrary, unfair, and violative of Article 12(1).
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, who had served the CWE for 26 years and was its General Manager since 1983, applied for a second extension of service after age 55. He said he had an outstanding record and had been invited by the Chairman himself to apply for the extension due to his ‘excellent service.’ His application was rejected on the basis of adverse comments made in two committee reports, even though he had never been informed of any allegations, never summoned, and never given a hearing. He claimed the refusal was arbitrary, unfair, and a violation of his rights under Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents argued that extension of service beyond age 55 is not a right but a matter entirely within the discretion of the Board and the Minister. They claimed the Board was entitled to rely on the adverse observations in the Parliamentary Committee Report and the A. L. M. Fernando Committee Report and therefore acted properly in refusing the extension.
interpretation_summary: The Court held that although extension beyond 55 is discretionary, once an employee applies, the authority must consider the application fairly, properly, and on a rational basis. The Board rejected the petitioner’s extension solely due to adverse findings in two committee reports. Yet the petitioner had never been summoned by those committees, never told of any allegations, and never given an opportunity to explain or defend himself. This violated the fundamental rule of natural justice—the audi alteram partem rule (the right to be heard). The Court emphasized that discretion cannot be exercised arbitrarily. The denial of a hearing rendered the decision unfair, irrational, and without a proper foundation. The Court distinguished earlier cases (Somipala and Perera) because those cases had not raised the issue of total denial of a hearing.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the refusal of the extension was unfair, arbitrary, lacked a rational basis, and violated Article 12(1). The Court granted relief and ordered the CWE to pay the petitioner Rs. 80,000 as compensation and Rs. 20,000 as costs.
principles_established: Even when a benefit is discretionary, the applicant is entitled to a fair and proper consideration.
Natural justice (audi alteram partem) applies even when the decision is not disciplinary—it applies whenever adverse findings are used to the detriment of a person.
Discretion must be exercised reasonably, fairly, and based on legitimate grounds.
A decision based on adverse material without giving the affected person a hearing is arbitrary and violates Article 12(1).
Fairness is a core component of equality under Article 12.
precedents_cited: Cooper v. Wandsworth Board of Works (1863) 14 C.B. (N.S.) 180
Shaughnessy v. United States 345 U.S. 206 (1953)
John v. Rees (1970) Ch. 345 at 402
Pinnawala v. Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation Ltd. (1997) 3 Sri LR 85
Dissanayake v. Kaleel (1993) 2 Sri LR 135
full_text:
AMERASINGHE v. BOARD OF DIRECTORS, CO-OPERATIVE WHOLESALE ESTABLISHMENT AND OTHERS
SUPREME COURT
G. P. S. DE SILVA, CJ, ANANDACOOMARASWAMY, J. AND GUNASEKERA, J.
S.C. APPLICATION NO. FR. 663/96
NOVEMBER 3, 1997; FEBRUARY 12, MARCH 29, APRIL 15, 1998.
Fundamental Rights - Extension of Services - Refusal of the application on the ground of adverse observations against the officer - Natural Justice - Right to a due consideration of the application - Article 12 (1) of the Constitution.
The petitioner who had 26 years' of meritorious service in the Co-operative Wholesale Establishment and who had been its General Manager since 1.9.83 was refused his second extension of service at the age of 56 years. The Board of Directors decided against the extension on account of "adverse observations" and "adverse references" made to the petitioner in two reports, namely the report of the Committee of 9 Members of Parliament and the A. L. M. Fernando Committee. The petitioner was never summoned or questioned by those Committees; nor was he given an opportunity of explaining in respect of which the Committees made "adverse observations" or "adverse references". He was not given any hearing at all on matters which he may well have been in a position to explain.
Held:
1. Even though the petitioner cannot claim as of right an extension of service beyond 55 years and the extension is a matter of discretion, once he makes an application, he is entitled to have his application properly, duly and fairly considered by the relevant authority.
2. On the facts and circumstances of the case, the exercise of the discretion was unfair, arbitrary, devoid of rational basis and violative of Article 12 (1) of the Constitution.
Cases referred to:
Cooper v. Wandsworth Board of Works (1863) 14 C.B. (N.S.) 180.
Shaughnessy v. United States 345 US 206 (1953).
John v. Rees (1970) Ch. 345 at 402.
Pinnawala v. Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation Ltd. (1997) 3 Sri LR 85.
Dissanayake v. Kaleel (1993) 2 Sri LR 135, 184.
Somipala v. The Board of Directors of the CWE SC Application 694/96 SC Minutes 8 July 1997 - distinguished.
Perera v. The Board of Directors, CWE SC Application 688/96 SC Minutes 6 October 1997 - distinguished.
APPLICATION for relief for infringement of fundamental rights.
S. L. Gunasekara with Manohara R. de Silva and W. D. Weeraratne for the petitioner.
Shibly Aziz, P.C. with S. S. Sahabandu and S. A. C. Sabry for the 1st respondent.
S. Fernando, S.S.C. with S. Rajaratnam, S.C. for 2nd and 3rd respondents.
Cur. adv. vult.
May 4, 1998.
G. P. S. DE SILVA, CJ.
This application relates to the refusal of the 2nd extension of service sought by the petitioner who was the General Manager of the Co-operative Wholesale Establishment (CWE). He complained that the refusal of the extension of his period of service is violative of the fundamental right guaranteed to him in terms of Article 12 (1) of the Constitution. In his petition he averred that he joined the CWE on 1st April, 1970, as an Assistant Accountant; on 1.9.73 he was promoted to the post of Accountant; he was promoted as Senior Accountant on 1.9.74 and on 1.1.79 as Chief Internal Auditor. He assumed office as Finance Manager on 15.7.79. He was appointed to the post of General Manager on 1.9.83, a post which he held until the time of the refusal to grant him his 2nd extension of service. Thus it is seen that the petitioner was a career officer of the CWE with about 26 years' of service. He was a graduate of the University of Ceylon and a fellow of the Chartered Institute of Management Accountants, U.K. He reached the age of 55 years on the 6th of September, 1995. He was granted his 1st extension for a period of one year from 6.9.95. The 1st extension of his period of service ended on 5.9.96. He had a long period of meritorious service.
On 17.4.96 the then Chairman of the CWE invited the petitioner to apply for his 2nd extension of service in appreciation of the "excellent service" rendered by him (P9). The petitioner submitted his application for the 2nd extension of service on 5.6.96 along with the recommendation of the Medical Officer and the Acting Chairman of the CWE (P10) and (P10A). Despite reminders there was no response to this application until 2nd September, 1996, when the Chairman of the CWE summoned the petitioner to his office at 11.45 a.m. and requested him not to insist on his application for an extension of service. The Chairman had requested the petitioner to inform him of his decision before 2 p.m. the same day. The petitioner by letter dated 2nd September, 1996, P11(c), stated: "... I do not find any reason why I should not ask for an extension or why such extension should not be granted by the Board. In the circumstances, I urge that my application be approved/recommended at the Board meeting to be held at 2.30 p.m. today." On 6.9.96 the petitioner received a letter dated 5.9.96 (P11E) from the Chairman, CWE, stating: (i) that his application has been forwarded to the Ministry as the Minister is the authority to decide on the question of extension of service; (ii) that the decision of the Minister has not been received as yet; (iii) that the petitioner should hand over the files and all other papers and documents, cash, if any, and inventory items including the car.
Although P11E states that no decision has been arrived at in regard to the petitioner's application for his 2nd extension of service, yet P12 clearly shows that at the Board meeting held on 2.9.96 the petitioner's application was considered and refused. It is of the utmost importance to note that the reason for the refusal of the petitioner's application is set out in P12 and it reads thus: "Application for extension was considered by the Board and in view of the adverse observations made by the Parliamentary Committee appointed by the Hon. Minister of Internal and External Trade, Commerce and Food and the A. L. M. Fernando Committee, the Board regretted its inability to recommend the extension of service."
The Chairman of the CWE produced along with his affidavit the document 1R5 which is described as an "addendum to the minutes of the meeting held on 2.9.96". 1R5, however, is dated 16.9.96 and it reads thus: "the Board decided as a matter of general policy not to grant any extension of service after the 55th year and also not to recommend such extension of service to the Ministry of Internal and External Trade, Commerce and Food in respect of the employees of the CWE in regard to whom any adverse reference had been made either by the Committee of the Hon. Members of Parliament or by the A. L. M. Fernando Committee and also by any other Committee of inquiry appointed in respect of the CWE by the Hon. Minister. ... In view of the above decision the Board decided not to recommend ... the extension of service of Mr. G. K. J. Amarasinghe (petitioner)."
Thus on a consideration of P12 and 1R5 it is clear that the Board decided not to recommend the extension of the period of service of the petitioner on account of the "adverse observations" and the "adverse references" made to the petitioner in the two reports, namely, the report of the Committee of 9 Members of Parliament and the report of the Committee headed by Mr. A. L. M. Fernando. However, it is not disputed that neither the Committee consisting of 9 Members of Parliament nor the A. L. M. Fernando Committee ever summoned the petitioner as a witness or in any other capacity; he was never questioned in regard to any allegation made against him; at no time was he made aware of any allegation against him; at no stage was the petitioner given an opportunity to explain matters in respect of which the Committee made "adverse observations" or "adverse references". In short he was given no hearing at all on matters which he may well have been in a position to explain.
While it is true, and contended for by Mr. Aziz, counsel for the 1st respondent, that the petitioner cannot claim as of right an extension of service beyond the 55th year, yet, in my view, once he makes an application he is entitled to have his application properly, duly and fairly considered by the relevant authority. Extension of service is no doubt a matter which falls within the discretion of the authority concerned, yet the discretion must be exercised reasonably, fairly and on legitimate grounds. On a consideration of the totality of the material on record, the conclusion is irresistible that the refusal of the petitioner's application for an extension of his period of service (on the basis of "adverse observations" and "adverse references" made by the two Committees of Inquiry) was in violation of the audi alteram partem rule. It was submitted by Mr. Aziz that the audi alteram partem rule would have applied only if disciplinary proceedings were taken against the petitioner and the refusal of his extension of the period of service was based on the findings reached against him at such disciplinary proceedings. With this submission I do not agree. In the words of Willes, J. in Cooper v. Wandsworth Board of Works: "... the rule is of universal application, and founded on the plainest principles of justice." Again, as observed by Jackson, J. in Shaughnessy v. United States: "Procedural fairness and regularity are of the indispensable essence of liberty..." Megarry, J. in John v. Rees at 402 stated: "As everybody who has anything to do with the law well knows, the path of the law is strewn with examples of open and shut cases which, somehow, were not; of unanswerable charges which, in the event, were completely answered; of inexplicable conduct which was fully explained..."
Mr. Aziz emphasised that the question of granting or refusing an extension of service is entirely a matter that falls within the discretion of the Board and the Minister. But what is relevant and important in the facts and circumstances of the present case is that the discretion has not been fairly, properly and duly exercised. The petitioner having been denied altogether a hearing before the Committees of Inquiry, I hold that the exercise of the discretion by the authorities was unfair, arbitrary, devoid of a rational basis, and was violative of Article 12 (1) (Pinnawala v. The Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation Ltd. and others). As observed by Fernando, J. in Dissanayake v. Kaleel at 184, "An expansive rather than a restrictive interpretation of the protection afforded by the principles of natural justice is demanded by the equality provisions in Article 12 of the Constitution; fairness lies at the root of equality and equal protection."
Mr. Aziz relied on the case of Somipala v. The Board of Directors of the CWE. This decision was followed in Perera v. The Board of Directors, CWE. The petitioners in both these fundamental rights applications were officers of the CWE and their applications for the second extension of service were refused by the Board at its meeting held on 2.9.96. While the facts are the same as in the case before us, yet the point considered in the instant case, namely, the total denial of a hearing and the consequent arbitrary exercise of the discretion, was not raised in those two applications. I am, therefore, of the opinion that the ruling in the earlier applications can be clearly distinguished from the present case.
For these reasons I hold that the petitioner is entitled to a declaration that the fundamental right guaranteed to him in terms of Article 12 (1) has been infringed. I direct the first respondent (CWE) to pay the petitioner a sum of Rs. 80,000/- (eighty thousand) as compensation and a sum of Rs. 20,000/- (twenty thousand) as costs.
ANANDACOOMARASWAMY, J. - I agree.
GUNASEKERA, J. - I agree.
Relief granted.
source: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 663/96 (FR)

case_title: Athukorala v. Jayaratne and Others (1996)

clauses.text: No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any such grounds.

legal_issue: Whether the petitioner’s sudden transfer from the Hanwella Divisional Secretariat to Homagama, allegedly due to her political opinion and activities as an elected member of the Seethawaka Pradeshiya Sabha, violated the protection against discrimination under Article 12(2) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that she was transferred out of her station because she was an elected UNP member of the Seethawaka Pradeshiya Sabha, and that the 1st and 2nd respondents acted on political motives. She argued that the transfer violated section 3.7 of Chapter XXXII of the Establishments Code, which entitled her to work close to the Local Authority she represented. She alleged the transfer was discriminatory and intended to restrict her political participation.
respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the petitioner’s transfer was required to ensure neutral and impartial administration at the Hanwella Secretariat. They claimed there were complaints alleging she favoured her political supporters and discriminated against others in her official duties. The 2nd respondent maintained that the transfer was necessary to prevent partisan influence and was carried out within delegated transfer powers.
interpretation_summary: The Court held that no credible evidence of misconduct had been produced, and the alleged complaints were vague, undisclosed, and untested. Section 3.7 of the Establishments Code was intended to protect elected officers by allowing them to work near their Local Authority, not to justify transfers away from it. The Court found that the transfer was motivated by the respondents’ views about the petitioner’s political opinion and activities. Acting on undisclosed allegations without inquiry was arbitrary and violated Article 12(2).
outcome: The Court declared that the petitioner’s fundamental right under Article 12(2) had been infringed. It cancelled the transfer, ordered her reinstatement to the Hanwella Divisional Secretariat, and directed the 1st and 2nd respondents personally to pay Rs. 25,000 each as compensation and costs.
principles_established: A public officer who is an elected member of a Local Authority is entitled to serve near that Local Authority under section 3.7 of the Establishments Code.
Transfers motivated by political opinion constitute discrimination under Article 12(2).
Vague, undisclosed complaints cannot justify adverse administrative action.
Even non-disciplinary decisions must follow fairness and cannot be based on arbitrary or politically motivated reasoning.
Authorities cannot indirectly penalise an officer for exercising lawful political rights.
precedents_cited: Madurapperuma v. Attorney-General, SC 90/79, S.C. Minutes 05.02.1980
full_text:
The Petitioner, a clerk working at the Hanwella Divisional Secretariat, alleges that she was summarily transferred to the Homagama Divisional Secretariat in violation of her fundamental right under Article 12(2). She was, since October 1992, a member of the Seethawaka Pradeshiya Sabha representing the United National Party. The Hanwella Secretariat was within the territorial limits of that Sabha.

It is not in dispute that the power to transfer clerks, which is vested in the Governor of the Western Province Provincial Council, had been duly delegated by him to the Provincial Public Service Commission, which in turn duly sub-delegated that power to the 2nd Respondent, the Chief Secretary of the Provincial Council, in terms of section 32 of the Provincial Councils Act, No. 42 of 1987.

The 3rd and 4th Respondents, the Deputy Secretary (Administration) and the Director (Administration), acting on behalf of the 2nd Respondent sent the Petitioner a letter dated 31.10.95, transferring her with immediate effect to Homagama. It disclosed no reason and it stated that travelling expenses and allowances would not be paid. Among the persons to whom that letter was copied was the 1st Respondent, the Secretary, Ministry of Public Administration, reference being made to his fax message dated 30.10.95 (No. SPA/10).

The Petitioner alleged that the decision to transfer her was contrary to section 3.7 of Chapter XXXII of the Establishments Code, and that the decision taken by the 2nd to 4th Respondents was not their own independent decision but was upon a direction by the 1st Respondent, who, she says, had no power in law to transfer her. She claims that the transfer was effected because of her political opinion, in order to restrain her from fully participating in her duties as a member of the Pradeshiya Sabha.

The 1st Respondent admitted that he made a "request" for the Petitioner's transfer, but claimed that he did not "direct" it. He said that he did so consequent to several complaints that he received pertaining to her behaviour, alleging that in the discharge of her official duties and functions she blatantly favoured her political supporters and persons who shared her political ideologies whilst discriminating against those who belonged to other political parties. He stated that his primary concern was the allegation that the partisan conduct of the Petitioner was adversely affecting the rights of the general public in their day to day dealings with her. He went on to say that he was compelled to request her transfer since her conduct adversely affected the neutral administration of the Divisional Secretary's Office. He added, however, that he was unaware whether the transfer was effected based solely on his request.

The 2nd Respondent stated that he directed the transfer upon receiving the 1st Respondent's letter dated 30.10.95, which said that the Petitioner, having served over 8 years at Hanwella and being a Pradeshiya Sabha member within the same jurisdiction, would adversely affect the neutral administration of the Divisional Secretariat, and therefore requested her transfer to an adjoining Secretariat outside that Pradeshiya Sabha area.

He sought to explain his conduct by stating that the Petitioner's transfer was not a normal or punishment transfer but was necessary because her official conduct was detrimental to the smooth working and upkeep of discipline at the workplace. He alleged that in matters connected with Janasaviya grants, poor relief and welfare benefits, the Petitioner favoured her political supporters while harassing and discriminating against others. He referred to oral complaints and two written communications: a letter dated 17 May 1995 from the Minister of Co-operatives, Local Government, Provincial Councils and Home Affairs referring to a complaint by a Provincial Council member, and the communication dated 30 October 1995 from the Secretary of Public Administration. He stated that to avoid a breakdown in neutral administration and discipline he transferred her to Homagama, the closest Secretariat outside the Seethawaka Pradeshiya Sabha area.

Section 3.7 of Chapter XXXII of the Establishments Code provides that if an officer entitled to exercise political rights is elected a member of a Local Government body, he or she should be allowed the concession of serving in a station close to the office of that Local Authority, subject to exigencies of service and disciplinary requirements, and will not be subject to normal transfer rules while continuing as a member of that body.

The Court found it unfortunate that the 1st Respondent made serious allegations of blatant political favouritism without disclosing who made the complaints or providing particulars. His letter of 30.10.95 did not mention any complaints but only the possibility of a future conflict of interest. The 2nd Respondent's claim that he inferred the existence of complaints from that letter was rejected. The Court inferred that there had likely been undisclosed communications and that the transfer was virtually an automatic response to the 1st Respondent's intervention.

The affidavits of the 1st and 2nd Respondents regarding complaints were found unacceptable, except for the Minister's letter of 17.5.95, which was evidence only that a complaint had been made, not that it was true. No prompt investigation had been conducted, and the Petitioner had not been informed of any allegations, given particulars, or afforded any inquiry. The 2nd Respondent even implied guilt in his affidavit without initiating disciplinary proceedings, which the Court found improper. The transfer could not be justified on that basis.

It was argued that the transfer was to ensure impartial and efficient administration. The Court held that section 3.7 did not authorise transferring an elected member away from the area of the Local Authority; rather, it entitled such an officer to serve close to that area. Chapter XXXII sought to facilitate political rights of public officers, and what was done was the opposite of what section 3.7 intended. Therefore, section 3.7 did not authorise the Petitioner's transfer.

The Court concluded that the 1st and 2nd Respondents caused the transfer because of their views about the Petitioner's political opinion and activities. A later Public Administration Circular introducing a new version of section 3.7, which might have sanctioned such transfers, had no retrospective effect and was irrelevant to the Petitioner's case.

The Petitioner was entitled to a declaration that her fundamental right under Article 12(2) had been infringed by the 1st and 2nd Respondents. Her transfer was cancelled and the Respondents were directed to reinstate her at Hanwella forthwith. Each of the 1st and 2nd Respondents was ordered to pay the Petitioner Rs 25,000 as compensation and costs.
source: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, SC Application No. 645/95, decided on 20 September 1996

case_title: Bandara and Another v. Premachandra, Secretary, Ministry of Lands, Irrigation and Mahaweli Development and Others (1993)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the termination of the petitioners’ probationary appointments and training, based on their participation in trade union action and treated as vacation of post, was arbitrary, discriminatory, contrary to the Establishments Code, and in violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution, despite the ‘pleasure’ clause in Article 55(1).
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, selected as Class III Grade III Surveyors and placed on probation while following a four-year degree course at the Institute of Surveying and Mapping, claimed that their services and training were unlawfully terminated after they, following their union’s decision, submitted sick notes and joined a work-to-rule campaign. They argued that they were in fact treated as having vacated post without being informed of that basis, and were thereby denied their right under Chapter V, section 7:4 of the Establishments Code to submit explanations. They further claimed that they were singled out and punished more harshly than other surveyors and trainees who engaged in similar trade union action, and that the real reason for the action was their participation in lawful trade union activities, violating Article 12(1) and their freedoms of association and expression.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that, as probationers holding office at pleasure within Article 55(1), the petitioners’ appointments could be terminated ‘without assigning any reason’ under Chapter II, section 11:4 and Chapter V, section 6:2 of the Establishments Code. They argued that the petitioners’ conduct in absenting themselves after tendering sick notes, as part of the union campaign, amounted to serious indiscipline and misconduct justifying immediate termination, and that the safeguards in section 11:2:1 (guidance, warnings, opportunities to improve) did not apply in the face of such grave behaviour. They also sought to distinguish the petitioners from other officers and earlier batches, relying on the petitioners’ status as newly recruited salary-drawing students on a residential course and the practical difficulties and public inconvenience that would arise if similar sanctions were imposed on large numbers of serving officers.
interpretation_summary: The Court held that the petitioners’ letters of appointment expressly incorporated the Establishments Code, which gives probationers not only obligations but also procedural protections, including guidance, warnings, and fair evaluation before termination. The misconduct in submitting false sick notes could warrant disciplinary action, but it was of a type that should have been dealt with under the Code, not by an abrupt termination that bypassed its procedures. Examining the internal minutes and correspondence, the Court found that the Secretary’s decision was actually to treat the petitioners as having vacated post, not to dismiss them outright, and that by misinforming them that their services had been terminated, the Surveyor General improperly deprived them of their right under section 7:4 to submit explanations which might have led to reinstatement. On Article 55(1), the Court held that the ‘pleasure principle’ is expressly made subject to the Constitution, including Article 12, and cannot authorise arbitrary or discriminatory dismissal; rules made under Article 55(4) must also conform to the Constitution and the rule of law. The phrase ‘without assigning any reason’ in the Establishments Code was interpreted to mean that no reason need be communicated to the officer, but a valid reason justifying dismissal in terms of the Code must exist and can be examined when fundamental rights are invoked. The Court further held that the real motive for the action was the petitioners’ participation in trade union activity, as revealed by the subsequent insistence on an undertaking to abstain from union activity and public statements that they had been ‘dragged into’ the campaign. Comparing the treatment of the petitioners with earlier trainee batches and with other surveyors and officers who engaged in the same union action but faced no disciplinary sanctions, the Court found no rational basis for the harsher punishment imposed on the petitioners. This differential treatment was unreasonable, arbitrary, and discriminatory, and thus violated Article 12(1).
outcome: The Court held that the petitioners had not been lawfully dismissed by the proper authority, that they were wrongly denied their right to explain a deemed vacation of post, and that they were unlawfully prevented from resuming their studies and work for participating in trade union action. It declared that their fundamental rights under Article 12(1) had been infringed, ordered their reinstatement with effect from 7 December 1992, directed payment of arrears of salary from 21 December 1992, and allowed them to resume their degree course forthwith with seniority preserved over later entrants. The State was ordered to pay each petitioner Rs. 2,000 as compensation; no personal costs order was made against the 2nd respondent because of the petitioners’ own misconduct.
principles_established: Probationary public officers are subject to, and protected by, the Establishments Code; probation cannot be used to bypass procedural safeguards such as guidance, warnings, and the right to explain alleged vacation of post.
The ‘pleasure’ clause in Article 55(1) is subject to the Constitution, including Article 12, so dismissal at pleasure cannot be arbitrary, discriminatory, or inconsistent with equal protection.

Rules made under Article 55(4) and phrases like ‘without assigning any reason’ must be interpreted consistently with the rule of law; a lawful, Code-based reason must exist even if it is not communicated, and may be scrutinised in fundamental rights proceedings.

Where other officers and trainees who participated in similar industrial action are treated more leniently, imposing the severe sanction of dismissal on one group without a rational basis amounts to unreasonable and discriminatory treatment under Article 12(1).
Administrative labelling of a situation (e.g. ‘termination’ instead of ‘vacation of post’) cannot be used to deprive officers of procedural rights expressly provided by the Establishments Code.

Adverse action taken primarily because of participation in trade union activity, rather than because of proven misconduct assessed under proper procedures, is impermissible and attracts constitutional scrutiny.
precedents_cited: Abeywickrema v. Pathirana [1986] 1 Sri LR 120
Chandrasiri v. Attorney-General [1989] 1 Sri LR 115
Attorney-General v. De Keyser’s Royal Hotel [1920] AC 508
Perera v. Jayawickrema [1985] 1 Sri LR 285
De Alwis v. Gunawardena SC 7/87, S.C. Minutes of 28.03.1988
full_text:
On 30.7.92, the 22 Petitioners, together with 15 others, were selected (on the basis of G.C.E. (A.L.) performance) to follow a four-year residential course leading to the award of a Bachelor's Degree in Surveying Science, by the Institute of Surveying and Mapping, Diyatalawa ("ISM"), a Degree-Awarding Institute. Only Class III, Grade III Surveyors were eligible for that course, which commenced on 24.8.92. The 1st Respondent, the Secretary, Ministry of Lands, Irrigation and Mahaweli Development, issued letters of appointment (P3) dated 24.8.92 to each Petitioner, appointing him as a Class III Grade III Surveyor in the Sri Lanka Surveyors’ Service; appointment was stated to be on probation for a period to be notified (but this was not done); and was subject to termination with one month's notice for (a) failure to pass the degree examination of the ISM; (b) failure to obtain the required number of marks at the end of each quarter; (c) unsatisfactory conduct during probation; or (d) inefficiency during probation.

It was expressly stated in P3 that if the required language proficiency was acquired, and if service during probation was satisfactory, the appointment would be confirmed in terms of Chapter II, Section 11, of the Establishments Code. Shortly thereafter, the Petitioners became members of the Government Surveyors’ Association ("the Union"), a duly registered trade union, and with some difficulty obtained leave to attend the Annual General Meeting held in Colombo on 26.9.92; leave having been refused by the 3rd Respondent, the Director, ISM, at the last moment, the 2nd Respondent, the Surveyor-General, granted such leave.

That Union thereafter embarked on trade union action, in support of certain demands, commencing with a work-to-rule campaign from 7.12.92. The initial stage of the work-to-rule was an abstention from work for two weeks by all members, after submitting applications for sick leave for that fortnight. The Petitioners state that the first part of their course (a three-month intensive English Course) had been completed by the end of November 1992, and that the next stage was due to commence in January 1993, so that there was no work scheduled for them in December. It is not disputed that the disciplinary rules required the Petitioners to get written permission from their lecturer-in-charge in order to leave the ISM. The Petitioners state that in accordance with the prevailing practice, they made entries in a leave register maintained for the purpose; they also sent telegrams requesting leave on the ground of illness, and these were received before 11.12.92; they later sent medical certificates. It is virtually a certainty that none of the Petitioners were in fact ill, and that medical certificates had been obtained from medical practitioners who were either dishonest or deceived.

This Court will not condone the conduct of an employee who lies to, or otherwise deceives, his employer as to the reason for his failure to work, whether individually or collectively; that it was trade union action aggravates rather than mitigates such misconduct. An employer would be justified in taking disciplinary action in respect of such misconduct. However, without dealing with the Petitioners for that misconduct, the 1st and 2nd Respondents chose instead to take action against them for participation in trade union activity.

By letter dated 11.12.92 (P4) the 2nd Respondent informed the Petitioners that the 1st Respondent had terminated their services, and their course of studies, with effect from 7.12.92; no reason was stated. The documentary material later revealed inconsistencies regarding whether the decision was termination or treating them as having vacated post. I hold that the 1st Respondent’s decision was not to dismiss the Petitioners, but to treat them as having vacated post.

Chapter V, Section 7:1, of the Establishments Code provides that an officer who absents himself from duty without leave will be deemed to have vacated his post from the date of such absence and he should be informed accordingly at once. Section 7:4 enables the officer to submit an explanation; such explanation must be considered by the Disciplinary Authority. By incorrectly informing the Petitioners that their services had been terminated, the 2nd Respondent deprived the Petitioners of their right to submit an explanation in respect of their vacation of post.

The Petitioners submitted a petition dated 16.12.92 pleading that, without a proper understanding of the gravity of the matter and without an opportunity of obtaining advice from their parents and elders, they had complied with the decision of the Union. They reported for work on 21.12.92, but were not allowed to do so. On 5.1.93 two Petitioners interviewed the 2nd Respondent, who indicated willingness to reinstate them if they furnished a written undertaking to refrain from participating in trade union activities during the four-year training period and to devote themselves exclusively to educational activities. The Petitioners gave this undertaking by letter dated 6.1.93 (P10). I cannot accept the 2nd Respondent’s later denial of requesting such an undertaking.

It is quite clear that it was on account of participation in trade union activity that the 2nd Respondent informed the Petitioners that their services had been terminated.

Although it was contended that a probationary appointment could be terminated without assigning any reason, the misconduct of the Petitioners was such that it had to be dealt with under the Establishments Code. Section 11:2:1 was intended to apply even to serious acts, omissions, and faults which, if persisted in, would prevent confirmation. The Petitioners’ misconduct does not justify an exception to the Code.

Article 55(1) of the Constitution provides that public officers hold office at pleasure, subject to the provisions of the Constitution. However, dismissal, even by the Cabinet of Ministers, cannot be for a reason which violates Article 12. The pleasure principle is subject to the equality provision of Article 12 and mandates fairness and excludes arbitrariness. Powers of appointment and dismissal must be exercised in the public interest and governed by reason and not caprice.

I am of the view that in the Establishments Code "without assigning any reason" only means that no reason need be stated to the officer, but that a reason which in terms of the Code justifies dismissal must exist; and when the law requires disclosure of such reason, it will have to be disclosed, and if not disclosed, legal presumptions will be drawn. I hold that the Cabinet has only delegated a power to dismiss for cause, and according to a prescribed procedure.

The 2nd Respondent incorrectly informed the Petitioners that their services had been terminated and deprived them of their right to submit an explanation. On 21.12.92 they were not permitted to resume their work and studies. Such treatment denied them equal protection of the law.

Other trainee surveyors in previous years had engaged in similar trade union action and only suffered suspension of their training programmes for two weeks. In December 1992, about 80 probationary surveyors not being students at ISM, and about 1,000 other officers, participated in the same trade union campaign, but no disciplinary action was taken against them. There was no rational basis for the difference in treatment. If the others were so leniently treated, the Petitioners should have been subjected to a much lesser punishment than dismissal; dismissal was unreasonable, arbitrary and discriminatory.

It is quite clear that the purported dismissal of the Petitioners was on account of their participation in trade union activity, and not on account of misconduct as such. However, since relief is granted under Article 12(1), I refrain from granting relief under Article 14(1)(c) and (d).

I hold that the Petitioners had not been dismissed by the proper authority; that the 2nd Respondent improperly deprived them of their right under Chapter V, Section 7:4; that they were improperly and unlawfully prevented from resuming their studies and work; that action was taken against them not for misconduct but for participating in trade union activity; and that their fundamental rights under Article 12(1) have been violated. I order their reinstatement with effect from 7.12.92, with arrears of salary from 21.12.92; they will be entitled to resume their course of studies forthwith, retaining seniority over students subsequently admitted to that course of studies.

The State is directed to pay each Petitioner compensation in a sum of Rs. 2,000/- in respect of the infringement of Article 12(1).
source: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 213/93, decided on 16 August 1993

case_title: Dayarathna and Others v. Minister of Health and Indigenous Medicine and Others (1999)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the State’s change of policy which stopped the advertised Assistant Medical Practitioner (AMP) training programme, and diverted successful candidates to inferior para-medical/PHI courses, unlawfully frustrated their legitimate expectations and amounted to arbitrary and unequal treatment contrary to Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, all of whom possessed the required higher educational qualifications, applied in response to Gazette No. 923 of 10.05.1996 to follow the course of training for the examination leading to the certificate of competency as Assistant Medical Practitioners. They sat the competitive examination on 27.12.1996 and were placed so as to qualify for training, subject only to a routine interview to verify documents (birth certificate, citizenship, educational certificates). No interview was held and no AMP training was commenced. Instead, after the GMOA wrote on 18.12.1997 opposing the restarting of the AMP training and refusing to participate in it, the Minister sought Cabinet approval to fill AMP vacancies with medical graduates and, by circular F1 dated 20.08.1998, invited the petitioners to apply for training as Pharmacists, MLTs or PHIs. The petitioners claimed (1) this substituted offer was clearly inferior in status, training and future prospects (no eligibility to register to practise medicine and surgery under the Medical Ordinance), (2) they had a legitimate expectation, based on the Gazette scheme and past practice, that they would receive AMP training if they met the published criteria, and (3) denying them that training, while earlier similarly placed applicants had received it, was unreasonable, discriminatory and violated Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents, through the Secretary to the Ministry, argued that the original need for AMPs arose when there were insufficient medical graduates to serve in hospitals, but that now around 800 medical officers passed out annually and existing vacancies could only absorb them for about two more years. They said the Government had a responsibility to provide jobs to graduates trained at public expense, and that AMP posts had historically been trained and supervised almost entirely by graduate medical officers and consultants. The GMOA had formally stated that its members would not participate in future AMP training, making it impossible, in the respondents’ view, to conduct a suitable AMP programme. On this basis the Minister submitted a Cabinet Memorandum on 11.03.1998 proposing to fill existing and future AMP vacancies with graduate medical officers, and to give high-scoring AMP candidates the opportunity, if they wished, to follow para-medical or PHI training instead. They maintained that the change of policy, driven by manpower needs, graduate employment and lack of trainers, justified discontinuing the AMP course and that no violation of equality had occurred.
interpretation_summary: The Court first compared the AMP path with that of pharmacists, MLTs and PHIs. Under the Medical Ordinance, AMPs, after prescribed periods of efficient service and further hospital experience, are eligible to seek registration to practise medicine and surgery, whereas pharmacists, MLTs and PHIs can never obtain such registration. The educational entry standards and the content, duration and intensity of AMP training (basic medical sciences, clinical subjects, extensive clinicals and clerkships) were significantly higher than those for the para-medical and PHI courses. On this basis, the Court held that inviting candidates who had already successfully competed for AMP training to instead apply for these other courses amounted to treating unequals as equals and was manifestly unreasonable and unfair. The Court also noted that earlier applicants in the same position (under previous intakes) had been given AMP training according to the same type of advertised scheme, so the departure in the petitioners’ case created discrimination between persons similarly situated without justification. Turning to legitimate expectation, the Court held that the Gazette notice, the structured scheme of competitive exam plus interview, and the consistent past practice created more than a mere hope: the petitioners had a legitimate expectation that, upon satisfying the stated conditions, they would be provided with the AMP training scheme advertised. The executive is free to change policy, but that freedom is not absolute. A change of policy that frustrates such an expectation must be (a) procedurally fair, giving affected persons an opportunity to be heard, and (b) substantively justified by overriding public interest, with means proportionate to the aim. Here, the only real driver of the policy shift was the GMOA’s refusal to cooperate and its demand that AMP training not restart, coupled with a preference to use the vacancies for medical graduates. The views of AMPs or of the petitioners were never sought; there was no structured weighing of their interests against a clearly articulated public interest. No Gazette or circular formally announced a change of policy; instead, the process simply stalled and was then redirected through F1. The Court rejected the idea that such union pressure and administrative convenience amounted to overriding public interest. It held that both the failure to give the petitioners a say and the decision to sacrifice their legitimate expectations solely to accommodate one professional group’s preferences were inconsistent with the equality guarantee and the rule-of-law values underlying Article 12.
outcome: The Court declared that the petitioners’ fundamental rights under Article 12(1) had been violated by the second respondent and held that the petitioners’ legitimate expectations regarding the AMP training scheme survived the purported policy change. Document F1 of 20.08.1998 was declared to be of no force or effect in law as against the petitioners. The Court ordered the first, second and third respondents to (a) hold the interview contemplated in Gazette No. 923 of 10.05.1996 within eight weeks of the judgment, and (b) provide the advertised AMP training scheme commencing within a reasonable time not exceeding six months from the date of the order. The State was directed to pay each petitioner Rs. 5,000 as costs.
principles_established: Legitimate expectation: Where the State, by Gazette, established procedures and benefits and has consistently acted in accordance with them, applicants who meet the criteria can acquire a legitimate expectation of the promised training or benefit, not merely a hope.

Policy change and fairness: While Government may change policy, it must consider and, where appropriate, protect legitimate expectations. When a change of policy will adversely affect specific individuals, they must be given an opportunity to be heard on why the new policy should not operate unfairly against them.

Article 12 and procedural fairness: Procedural rights (like the right to be heard before a detrimental policy change is applied) are closely tied to Article 12’s guarantee of equality, helping ensure objectivity, impartiality and similar treatment of like cases.

Overriding public interest requirement: A change of policy that frustrates legitimate expectations may only be justified where an overriding public interest is demonstrated, and even then the means chosen must be proportionate. Mere pressure from a professional group or administrative convenience is insufficient.

Substantive equality: Article 12 requires substantive as well as formal equality. Treating individuals who have qualified for a higher professional track as if they were candidates for lower-tier para-medical courses amounts to treating unequals as equals and can be unconstitutional.

Consistent treatment of similarly situated persons: When earlier candidates with similar qualifications were given AMP training under a comparable scheme, later candidates cannot be arbitrarily denied the same path without an objectively reasonable and proportionate justification.
precedents_cited: R v. Hertfordshire County Council, ex p. Cheung (The Times, 4 April 1986)
R v. MAFF, ex p. Hamble (Offshore Fisheries Ltd.) (1995) 2 All ER 714
