full_text:
DAYARATHNA AND OTHERS v. MINISTER OF HEALTH AND INDIGENOUS MEDICINE AND OTHERS
SUPREME COURT
AMERASINGHE, J., GUNASEKERA, J. AND WEERASEKARA, J.
S.C. APPLICATIONS NOS. 513–528/98
APRIL 1, 1999.

Fundamental Rights – Legitimate expectation – Change of Government policy – Duty to act fairly and in the public interest – Denial of expectations – Violation of the right to equality – Article 12(1) of the Constitution.

By notification in the Gazette dated 10.05.1996 the Ministry of Health called for applications from persons desirous of following a course of training leading to the award of the certificate of competency as Assistant Medical Officers. Fifteen petitioners who were eligible for enrolment to follow the course of training applied in response to the notification and sat a competitive examination conducted on 27.12.1996; and they were so placed on the results of the examination as to be qualified to follow the course of training. According to the scheme published in the Gazette, the next step was the holding of an interview to check the qualifications, meaning the checking of (1) the birth certificate, (2) evidence of citizenship, and (3) certificates relating to educational qualifications. That interview was not held.

Then, on 18.12.1997 the Secretary, Government Medical Officers' Association (GMOA) informed the Minister of Health and Indigenous Medicine that they desired the provision of employment to medical graduates and saw no justification "to restart the AMP training course"; and that their members "would not participate in any component of the training programme". Thereupon, on 11.03.1998 the Minister sought Cabinet approval to fill the existing and future vacancies in the cadre of Assistant Medical Practitioners with Medical Graduates and to offer the petitioners the option of following the course for para medical services/Public Health Inspectors, if they so desired. By a circular letter dated 20.08.1998, the petitioners were invited to apply for training as Pharmacists, Medical Laboratory Technologists and Public Health Inspectors.

The requisite qualifications for such training and the course subjects are less than what are required for the AMP course. Besides, persons serving in Para Medical Services and as Public Health Inspectors are not eligible to seek registration under the Medical Ordinance to practise medicine and surgery whilst Assistant Medical Practitioners are eligible to seek such registration, subject to certain conditions.

Held:
On the facts of the case, the petitioners had a legitimate expectation that they would, upon satisfying prescribed conditions, be provided with a course of training for the examination leading to the award of the certificate of competency as Assistant Medical Practitioners. The decision effecting a change of policy which destroyed the expectation of the petitioners did not depend upon considerations of public interest. In deciding upon the conflicting interests of Graduate Medical Officers and Assistant Medical Practitioners, the 1st, 2nd and 3rd respondents considered the views of the GMOA and yielded to their pressure. Neither the views of the Assistant Medical Practitioners nor those of the petitioners were sought. Hence, the rights of the petitioners guaranteed by Article 12(1) of the Constitution were violated.

Per Amerasinghe, J.:
"When a change of policy is likely to frustrate the legitimate expectation of individuals, they must be given an opportunity of stating why the change of policy should not affect them unfavourably. Such procedural rights have an important bearing on the protection afforded by Article 12 of the Constitution against unequal treatment, arbitrarily, invidiously, irrationally or otherwise unreasonably dealt out by the executive."

APPLICATION for relief for infringement of fundamental rights.
Romesh de Silva, PC with Geethaka Gunawardena for the petitioners.
Kolitha Dharmawardena, DSG with Viran Corea, SC for the respondents.
Cur. adv. vult.

May 4, 1999.
AMERASINGHE, J.

Sixteen petitioners filed separate applications alleging the violation of their respective fundamental rights guaranteed by Article 12(1) of the Constitution. Counsel agreed that, since these applications related to complaints arising from a single decision of the first, second and third respondents, they could be heard together and decided by a single judgment.

The Secretary of the Ministry of Health, Highways and Social Services by notification in Government Gazette No. 923 of 10.05.1996 called for applications from citizens of Sri Lanka who were "desirous of following a course of training for the examination leading to the award of the certificate of competency as Assistant Medical Officers". It is not disputed that each of the petitioners possessed the stipulated qualifications, submitted applications, sat the competitive examination conducted on 27.12.1996, and were placed on the results so as to be qualified to follow the course of training.

Although paragraph 10 of the scheme published in Gazette No. 923 stated that the method of selection included an interview to check qualifications, no such interview was held, despite several inquiries from the petitioners.

Instead of proceeding with the advertised course of training, the petitioners were by circular letter dated 20.08.1998 invited to apply for training as Pharmacists, Medical Laboratory Technologists and Public Health Inspectors.

There are significant distinctions between those positions and Assistant Medical Practitioners, both regarding their standing and training, and eligibility for selection. Under section 41(2A) and 41(2B) of the Medical Ordinance, Assistant Medical Practitioners may, subject to conditions, be registered to practise medicine and surgery. Pharmacists, Medical Laboratory Technologists and Public Health Inspectors are not eligible for such registration.

The educational qualifications and training schemes also differ significantly. Assistant Medical Practitioner trainees undergo an intensive programme including Anatomy, Physiology, Biochemistry, Pharmacology, Pathology, Community Medicine, Medicine, Surgery, Paediatrics, Gynaecology and Obstetrics, together with extensive clinical exposure and internship. The training equips them with responsibilities including diagnosis, treatment, supervision of continuing care, and management of peripheral medical units. No such equivalence was suggested regarding the alternative para-medical training.

Having regard to the superior qualifications required, the more intensive training, and the petitioners’ success at a competitive examination qualifying them for AMP training, the invitation to apply for para-medical courses amounted to treating unequals equally and was manifestly unreasonable and unfair.

Moreover, earlier applicants similarly situated had been treated differently. It is a constitutional requirement that persons in a similar position be treated similarly. Article 12 requires substantive as well as formal equality.

The petitioners contended that their legitimate expectations had been disappointed. They sought relief including revocation of the decision in the letter dated 20.08.1998 and an order directing the respondents to hold the interview and conduct the AMP training course.

The respondents contended that the need for Assistant Medical Practitioners had diminished due to the increasing number of graduate medical officers and that the GMOA had refused to participate in training. The Minister submitted a Cabinet memorandum proposing that vacancies be filled by graduate doctors and that petitioners be offered para-medical training instead.

The Court observed that while governments may change policy, they are not free to ignore legitimate expectations without considering fairness and public interest. Here, no formal policy change had been publicly announced; rather, the change followed pressure from the GMOA. The views of the petitioners or Assistant Medical Practitioners were not sought.

The petitioners had a legitimate expectation based on the Gazette notification, established practice, and representations made. They were denied both a procedural opportunity to be heard and substantive fairness. No overriding public interest was shown to justify frustrating their expectations.

In these circumstances, the legitimate expectations of the petitioners survived the policy change.

I declare that the fundamental rights of the petitioners guaranteed by Article 12(1) of the Constitution have been violated by the second respondent. I further declare that the circular letter dated 20.08.1998 is of no force or avail in law as far as the petitioners are concerned.

I order that in respect of each petitioner the first, second and third respondents shall:
(a) hold the interview referred to in Government Gazette No. 923 of 10.05.1996 within eight weeks from the date of this judgment; and
(b) provide the scheme of training advertised in Gazette No. 923 of 10.05.1996 commencing within a reasonable time not exceeding six months from the date of this order.

I further order that the State shall pay each petitioner a sum of Rs. 5,000 as costs.

GUNASEKERA, J. – I agree.
WEERASEKERA, J. – I agree.

Relief granted.
source: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Applications Nos. 513–528/98, decided on 4 May 1999

case_title: Dharmaratne and Another v. Sri Lanka Export Development Board and Others (1995)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the promotion of certain Assistant Directors to the post of Deputy Director Grade 2 by the Sri Lanka Export Development Board, based on an interview and internally-set criteria, was arbitrary and irrational so as to amount to unequal treatment and a violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, both Assistant Directors of the Sri Lanka Export Development Board, applied for promotion to Deputy Director Grade 2 after vacancies were advertised in March 1993. An interview board (2nd–6th respondents) interviewed internal and external candidates. The 7th–12th respondents (internal) and 13th respondent (external) were appointed; the petitioners were not. The petitioners did not contest the external appointment (13th respondent), but alleged that the promotions of the 7th–12th respondents were arbitrary and discriminatory. They argued that (1) there was no proper scheme of recruitment or promotion in force, and the older scheme (P1) with performance evaluation was ignored; (2) the criteria used by the interview board were ad hoc, vague and subjective; (3) insufficient weight was given to seniority, as only one mark per year in Grade 3 was awarded, instead of seniority getting about one-third of the total marks; (4) there was no proper mechanism or appraisal system in place to assess experience, performance and managerial ability; and (5) too much weight was given to interview performance and communication skills, which they said were inherently subjective. They also alleged political pressure and claimed they had been treated unequally compared to the selected officers.
respondent_argument: The 7th–12th respondents (promoted internal candidates) and the 2nd respondent (Chairman of the Board, and head of the interview panel) contended that the earlier 1985 promotion scheme and the 1984 evaluation process relied on by the petitioners had been abandoned as unsatisfactory, and that the applicable framework was based on Public Administration Circular No. 15/90 and the Board’s later documents (2R2–2R3). The posts of Deputy Director were senior managerial positions requiring strong management, coordination and staff-supervision abilities, not merely seniority. The interview board therefore adopted a set of criteria: (1) seniority (one mark per year in Grade 3), (2) additional job-oriented qualifications (diplomas, MSc/MBA, PhD), (3) experience in relevant areas (export development, marketing, project appraisal, planning etc.), (4) performance (ability to identify, analyse and solve problems with practical solutions), (5) communication skills (clarity, correct language, coherent presentation) and (6) managerial ability (assessed partly by consulting the directors/head of each candidate’s division). They produced a mark sheet (2R5) showing each candidate’s scores under these heads, according to which the 7th–12th respondents scored higher overall than the petitioners (who scored 34 and 33). They argued that the process was structured, multi-factorial, reasonably objective in most criteria, and that there was no political interference. They claimed the difference in outcome was due to relative merit and suitability, not discrimination.
interpretation_summary: The Court first examined the structure and composition of the interview board and the nature of the criteria used. The board included the Chairman and senior directors of the EDB who were familiar with the organisation and the Assistant Directors from whom the internal candidates came. The board had in advance detailed schedules of each candidate’s data and each member made notes on these during the interviews. Looking criterion by criterion (as per the mark sheet 2R5), the Court held that seniority and additional qualifications were fully objective, being derived directly from service records and certificates. Experience, assessed by looking at actual work done in export development, marketing, project appraisal, entrepreneur development, planning and trade information, was also capable of objective assessment. Performance was evaluated on concrete aspects: problem identification, understanding of subject matter, analysis, use of current data and statistics, and ability to propose practical solutions. Communication skills were judged by clarity of speech, correct language use, and the coherent presentation of ideas. The Court found these criteria to be clear, relevant and not capricious. The only area with greater subjectivity was managerial ability, but for this the board had filled the gap created by the abandonment of the earlier evaluation scheme by consulting the directors of the divisions where candidates worked. The Court accepted this evidence and viewed it as a responsible way to assess day-to-day managerial capability. On this basis, the Court concluded that while the system was not perfect, the overall process was responsible and not arbitrary. On the complaint about lack of a formal promotion scheme and prior disclosure of criteria, the Court (per Fernando J.) observed that, although it is desirable that criteria and weightage be laid down and disclosed beforehand, failure to do so is not automatically fatal, and in the absence of an established scheme the interview board could legitimately formulate relevant criteria and weightage. The chosen criteria—seniority, additional relevant qualifications, experience, performance, communication skills and managerial ability—were all relevant and comprehensive; no crucial factor had been excluded. The contention that too little weight was given to seniority and too much to interview performance was rejected: weightage is a matter for the interview board’s discretion, especially for senior posts where merit, ability and performance rightly carry heavier emphasis. Further, the Court pointed out that seniority was indirectly reflected again through the experience criterion. On the argument that, without an annual performance appraisal system, performance and managerial ability could not be properly assessed, the Court held that while such a system is highly desirable and may in future become effectively mandatory in practice, it is not presently a legal requirement. In its absence, the board had to make the best possible assessment and could not be faulted simply for operating without a formal appraisal system. The Court found no evidence of mala fides, political interference, abuse of discretion or irrationality in the board’s decisions.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioners had not established that the promotion decisions were arbitrary, capricious or irrational. There was no violation of their fundamental right to equality and equal protection under Article 12(1). The application was dismissed, and the appointments/promotions of the 7th–12th respondents stood undisturbed.
principles_established: Promotion and equality: For a violation of Article 12(1) in promotion cases, it is not enough to show dissatisfaction with the outcome; the decision-making process must be shown to be arbitrary, irrational, capricious or tainted by mala fides or irrelevant considerations.

Criteria and subjectivity: Selection for senior posts may legitimately include subjective elements (e.g., performance, communication skills, managerial ability) as long as the criteria are relevant, clearly defined, and applied in good faith without arbitrariness.

Weightage discretion: The allocation of weight between seniority and merit-related factors is primarily a matter for the decision-maker’s discretion. For posts with greater responsibilities, stronger emphasis on merit, performance and ability is justified, and giving seniority a modest direct weight is not inherently unreasonable, especially where it is also reflected indirectly through experience.

Absence of formal appraisal scheme: Although an annual performance appraisal system is very desirable and may become standard in industrial relations practice, its absence does not automatically invalidate a promotion decision if performance, experience and managerial ability are otherwise reasonably assessed.

Prior disclosure of criteria: It is desirable but not mandatory that criteria and weightage be disclosed to candidates in advance; failure to do so will only be fatal where it leads to unfairness, irrationality or discrimination on the facts of the case.

Judicial deference in promotion decisions: Courts will not re-mark candidates or substitute their own view of appropriate weightage and scores for that of a competent interview board in the absence of evidence of bad faith, abuse of power or manifest unreasonableness.

SC Dayarathna and Others v. Minister of Health and Indigenous Medicine and Others
DAYARATHNA AND OTHERS v. MINISTER OF HEALTH AND INDIGENOUS MEDICINE AND OTHERS
SUPREME COURT
AMERASINGHE, J., GUNASEKERA, J. AND WEERASEKARA, J.
S.C. APPLICATIONS NOS. 513-528/98
APRIL 1, 1999.
Fundamental Rights - Legitimate expectation - Change of Government policy - Duty to act fairly and in the public interest - Denial of expectations - Violation of the right to equality - Article 12 (1) of the Constitution.
By notification in the Gazette dated 10.05.1996 the Ministry of Health called for applications from persons desirous of following a course of training leading to the award of the certificate of competency as Assistant Medical Officers. Fifteen petitioners who were eligible for enrolment to follow the course of training applied in response to the notification and sat a competitive examination conducted on 27.12.1996; and they were so placed on the results of the examination as to be qualified to follow the course of training. According to the scheme published in the Gazette, the next step was the holding of an interview to check the qualifications, meaning the checking of (1) the birth certificate, (2) evidence of citizenship, and (3) certificates relating to educational qualifications. That interview was not held. Then, on 18.12.1997 the Secretary, Government Medical Officers' Association (GMOA) informed the Minister of Health and Indigenous Medicine that they desired the provision of employment to medical graduates and saw no justification "to restart the AMP training course"; and that their members "would not participate in any component of the training programme". Whereupon, on 11.03.1998 the Minister sought cabinet approval to fill the existing and future vacancies in the cadre of Assistant Medical Practitioners with Medical Graduates and to offer the petitioners the option of following the course for para medical services/Public Health Inspectors, if they so desire; and by a circular letter dated 20.08.1998, the petitioners were invited to apply for training as Pharmacists, Medical Laboratory Technologists and Public Health Inspectors. The requisite qualifications for such training and the course subjects are less than what are required for the AMP course. Besides, persons serving in Para Medical Services and as Public Health Inspectors are not eligible to seek registration under the Medical Ordinance to practise medicine and surgery whilst Assistant Medical Practitioners are eligible to seek such registration, subject to certain conditions.
Held: On the facts of the case, the petitioners had a legitimate expectation that they would, upon satisfying prescribed conditions, be provided with a course of training for the examination leading to the award of the certificate of competency as Assistant Medical Practitioners. The decision effecting a change of policy which destroyed the expectation of the petitioners did not depend upon considerations of public interest. In deciding upon the conflicting interests of Graduate Medical Officers and Assistant Medical Practitioners, the 1st, 2nd and 3rd respondents (the Minister, his Secretary and the Deputy Director General Administration, respectively) considered the views of the GMOA and yielded to their pressure. Neither the views of the Assistant Medical Practitioners nor those of the petitioners were sought. Hence, rights of the petitioners guaranteed by Article 12 (1) of the Constitution were violated.
Per Amerasinghe, J.: "When a change of policy is likely to frustrate the legitimate expectation of individuals, they must be given an opportunity of stating why the change of policy should not affect them unfavourably. Such procedural rights have an important bearing on the protection afforded by Article 12 of the Constitution against unequal treatment, arbitrarily, invidiously, irrationally or otherwise unreasonably dealt out by the executive."
Cases referred to include R. v. Hertfordshire C.C., ex P. Cheung; R. v. MAFF ex. P. Hamble (Offshore Fisheries Ltd.); R. v. Secretary of State for the Home Dept., ex P. Ruddock; Findlay v. Secretary of State for the Home Dept.; Council of Civil Service Union v. Minister for Civil Services; Hughes v. Dept, of Health and Social Security; HTV Ltd. v. Price Commission; Preston v. IRC; Attorney-General for New South Wales v. Quin; Att-Gen of Hong Kong v. Ng Yen Shin; Re Findlay; Robertson v. Minister of Pensions; Lever Finance Ltd. v. Westminster (City) London Borough Council; Associated Pictures Houses Ltd. v. Wednesbury Corpn; Rex v. Secretary of State of the Home Dept., ex. P. Khan.
APPLICATION for relief for infringement of fundamental rights. Romesh de Silva, PC with Geethaka Gunawardena for the petitioner. Kolitha Dharmawardena, DSG with Viran Corea, SC for the respondents. Cur. adv. vult. May 4, 1999.
AMERASINGHE, J.: Sixteen petitioners filed separate applications alleging the violation of their respective fundamental rights guaranteed by Article 12 (1) of the Constitution. Learned counsel for the petitioners and respondents submitted that, since these applications related to complaints arising from a single decision of the first, second and third respondents, the several applications may be heard together and that a single judgment would be applicable as far each of the sixteen petitioners and four respondents were concerned. [Further detailed facts, affidavits, and procedural history describing the notification, examination, interviews, training courses, differences between AMP and paramedical training, and the respondents' actions.] 
On the basis of the facts, it was held that the petitioners' legitimate expectation had been violated. The Court declared that the fundamental rights of the petitioners guaranteed by Article 12 (1) of the Constitution had been violated by the second respondent; that document F1 dated 20.08.1998 is of no force or avail in law; and ordered that the first, second and third respondents hold the interviews within eight weeks and commence the AMP training scheme within six months. The State was directed to pay each petitioner Rs. 5,000 as costs. GUNASEKERA, J. and WEERASEKERA, J. agreed. Relief granted.

case_title: Gunaratne and Others v. Ceylon Petroleum Corporation and Others (1996)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation’s Board resolution summarily terminating the petitioners’ dealership agreement and cancelling their statutory authority under section 5E of the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation Act, and appointing a new dealer, constituted executive/administrative action which violated the petitioners’ right to equality under Article 12(1) of the Constitution; and whether fundamental rights review can apply only at the ‘threshold stage’ of a contract or also during its subsistence.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, four partners operating the Kottawa Lanka Filling Station, held a dealership agreement with the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation (CPC) signed by them on 23.03.1994 and by CPC on 26.10.1994, together with statutory authority under section 5E of the CPC Act to sell, supply and distribute Lanka Two Star petrol, diesel and lubricants. Prior to this, the 1st petitioner individually had held a similar dealership for many years at the same station. By letter dated 04.01.1996, signed by the CPC Marketing Manager (9th respondent), CPC summarily terminated the dealership agreement and cancelled the authority, and on the same day took over possession and handed the station to the 11th respondent as the new dealer, pursuant to a Board resolution. The letter referred to five earlier warning letters (1981, 1984, 1986, 1988 and 1995) and cited clause 12B of the agreement and section 5H(4) of the Act. The petitioners argued that: (a) the termination was arbitrary, based mainly on old incidents long predating the partnership agreement and involving only the 1st petitioner; (b) the 2nd–4th petitioners were being penalised for events which occurred before they became partners; (c) the most recent incident in 1995 (a defective pump and trainee pumper error) had already been investigated, the pumper dismissed, and the matter finally disposed of by a warning; (d) there were no valid fresh grounds to reopen it or to justify termination; (e) the CPC Marketing Manual prescribed a procedure for selecting new dealers (multiple applications, area-level evaluation, full Board paper comparing candidates) which had not been followed in appointing the 11th respondent; and (f) the Board had acted without giving the petitioners any hearing or notice, and without properly informing itself of the true factual position, thereby acting arbitrarily and in violation of Article 12(1). They sought relief for infringement of their fundamental rights arising from the termination and cancellation.
respondent_argument: On behalf of CPC (1st respondent) and its Chairman and Directors (2nd–8th respondents), it was contended that: (1) the Board’s decision to terminate the dealership and cancel the authority was a commercial decision in the exercise of contractual rights under a concluded contract and therefore did not constitute ‘executive or administrative action’ within Article 126; at most, only the initial award of the dealership could be subject to fundamental rights review at the ‘threshold stage’; (2) clause 12B of the dealership agreement and section 5H(4) of the CPC Act conferred extremely wide powers on the Board, including termination without notice and without assigning reasons, in the Board’s absolute discretion; (3) the termination was justified by the dealer’s past conduct, including the five warning letters cited (from 1981, 1984, 1986, 1988 and 1995) and other alleged instances of misconduct/inefficiency both before and after the 1994 agreement, such as pumps delivering short and dishonoured cheques; (4) the partnership was between the original dealer (1st petitioner) and his family members and they could not escape the consequences of his earlier conduct; and (5) the Board resolution lawfully combined termination of the existing dealership and appointment of the 11th respondent. The 11th respondent, for his part, argued that he had applied for a dealership in or about August 1995, been interviewed, and that CPC officials had investigated his suitability. He further submitted that the petitioners had neither pleaded that his appointment was wrongful nor sought any specific relief against his dealership as required by Rule 44(1)(d) of the Supreme Court Rules, and therefore no order should be made affecting his appointment.
interpretation_summary: The Court first examined whether the impugned Board resolution was ‘executive or administrative action’ reviewable under Article 126. It held that the supply and distribution of petroleum products by CPC is a governmental function, performed as agent of the State under statute (sections 5B, 5E, 5F of the CPC Act), and that the grant and cancellation of dealership authority is a statutory power, not a purely private commercial matter. The dealership agreement is intimately linked with the statutory authority under section 5E (and referable to section 5F), so decisions to enter into, continue or terminate such dealerships constitute executive/administrative action. Rejecting the ‘threshold stage’ argument, the Court held that Article 12’s equality guarantee applies not only when a contract is initially awarded but throughout its subsistence: the State cannot indirectly do, by termination, what it cannot directly do at the award stage (e.g. discriminate on political, racial or religious grounds). The principle of equality in Article 12 is rooted in the Rule of Law and prohibits arbitrary and discriminatory action; there is no carve-out for post-contract acts or for particular types of contracts. The Court distinguished Roberts v. Ratnayake, noting that the present case involves powers exercised under statute, and adopted a broader view that Article 12 applies to arbitrary actions generally, not only where particular statutory protections are engaged. Having found that the Board’s resolution was executive/administrative action, the Court then considered whether it was arbitrary or discriminatory. Although clause 12B and section 5H(4) appear to confer powers to terminate without notice and ‘without assigning any reasons’ and to cancel authority in ‘absolute discretion’, these powers are held in trust for the public and must be exercised reasonably and for proper purposes. Even if reasons need not be stated at the time of termination, when the decision is challenged the burden lies on CPC to justify it with sufficient cause. The Court scrutinised the grounds invoked. It held that neither clause 12B nor section 5H(4) permitted reliance on conduct occurring before the grant of the current dealership/authority (save perhaps for unknown facts later discovered); otherwise, 2nd–4th petitioners would be punished for events when they had no control or responsibility. Therefore, the four older warning letters (1981, 1984, 1986, 1988) could not be used to justify termination of the 1994 partnership dealership. As to post-1994 conduct: (a) incidents where pumps delivered less were primarily attributable to CPC, as the pumps were CPC’s property, CPC was responsible for proper calibration, and dealers were not supposed to tamper with them. Some inspection reports even showed over-delivery. It would have been unreasonable to terminate on this basis, and in any event the Board paper did not rely on these incidents, so they could not retrospectively justify the decision; (b) dishonoured cheques issued in late December 1995 / early January 1996 could not serve as a ground either. The timing suggested that some cheques may have been presented after the forced takeover on 04.01.1996; CPC had promised to pay for stocks taken over (worth about Rs 577,587) but had not done so, and had taken no legal action regarding the cheques. There was no evidence that this issue influenced the Board’s decision; (c) the only incident clearly relied on was that behind the fifth warning letter dated 29.06.1995, where a pump sometimes failed to return to zero and a trainee pumper attempted to dispense fuel improperly. The defect had been promptly reported to CPC; the pumper was dismissed; and CPC had expressly decided not to take disciplinary action but only to warn, stating that future irregularities would be reported to the Board. The Court held that, given CPC’s responsibility for maintaining its own pumps, this single incident, already dealt with, was insufficient to justify termination. The Board had not been informed that four of the five warnings predated the current partnership and the involvement of 2nd–4th petitioners, and that the remaining incident had been concluded. The Directors had not sworn that they would have terminated solely on that single incident or without any reason. On this basis, the Court concluded that the Board’s decision to summarily terminate the agreement and cancel the authority lacked a rational foundation and was arbitrary. Regarding the structure of the Board resolution, the Court treated it as containing two limbs: (1) termination of the existing dealership and cancellation of the authority; (2) appointment of the 11th respondent as the new dealer with fresh authority. While the two limbs were distinct and severable, the first limb itself (agreement + authority) was not severable because the two were inextricably linked. The first limb was therefore invalid in its entirety for violating Article 12(1). As to the second limb, the Court noted that the marketing manual procedure for selecting new dealers had not been followed and that there was no clear evidence as to how the 11th respondent was chosen. However, since the petitioners had not pleaded that the 11th respondent’s appointment was unlawful nor prayed for any specific relief against his dealership, and because he had not been put clearly on notice that his appointment was in jeopardy, the Court held it would not be just and equitable to disturb his dealership in these proceedings. Instead, it confined relief to the unlawful termination and cancellation affecting the petitioners and compensated them for the resulting loss.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the Board’s resolution terminating the petitioners’ dealership agreement and cancelling their statutory authority constituted executive/administrative action and that, in doing so arbitrarily and without proper grounds, the 1st–8th respondents had violated the petitioners’ fundamental right to equality under Article 12(1). The termination and cancellation (the first limb of the resolution) were declared invalid as against the petitioners. However, the Court declined to make any order affecting the appointment of the 11th respondent as the new dealer, due to the absence of proper pleadings and prayer. The Court awarded the petitioners (collectively) Rs. 75,000 as compensation and costs for the infringement and, recognising that a lawful three-month termination with notice would have yielded further profits, directed the 1st respondent, at its option, either (a) to grant the petitioners, within six months, a dealership in respect of the same filling station or another mutually acceptable station, or (b) to pay them an additional Rs. 500,000 as compensation for lost profits.
principles_established: Executive/administrative character of statutory contracts: Where a public corporation exercises statutory powers to grant and cancel authorities (e.g. exclusive statutory rights to sell and distribute petroleum) and enters into closely linked contracts (dealership agreements) for that purpose, its decisions to grant, continue or terminate such arrangements constitute ‘executive or administrative action’ subject to fundamental rights review, and are not purely private commercial decisions.

No ‘threshold only’ limitation: Fundamental rights constraints under Article 12 apply not only at the initial or ‘threshold’ stage of awarding a contract, licence or dealership, but also throughout its subsistence. The State cannot evade equality obligations by using termination or cancellation after award to achieve discriminatory or arbitrary outcomes it could not justify at the award stage.

Article 12 and the Rule of Law: Article 12 embodies a broad principle of equality before the law as part of the Rule of Law underpinning the Constitution. It prohibits arbitrary, capricious or discriminatory action even where a power is framed in terms of ‘absolute discretion’ or ‘without assigning any reasons’, especially where that power is exercised under statute.

Limits on wide termination powers: Contractual clauses and statutory provisions which allow termination ‘without notice’ or ‘without assigning any reasons’ and cancellation of authority in ‘absolute discretion’ cannot be read as conferring unfettered, arbitrary power. Even if reasons need not be stated initially, valid reasons must exist and can be scrutinised by the Court; reliance on stale, irrelevant, or previously concluded matters, or on facts predating the current contractual relationship, is impermissible where it unfairly prejudices new parties.

Temporal relevance of misconduct: In assessing whether misconduct justifies termination of a later partnership or contract, acts occurring prior to the grant of the current agreement/authority cannot generally be used against parties who were not then responsible or in control, except possibly where such facts were unknown at the time of grant and later discovered.

Duty to maintain fairness in commercial-type public dealings: Even where the State or a public corporation is engaged in commercial activities (e.g. running filling stations), its decisions, particularly those grounded in statutory monopolies and public functions, must meet standards of fairness and rationality; powers are held in trust for the public and cannot be exercised for improper or arbitrary reasons.

Severability in relief: Where a single resolution combines both an unlawful termination/cancellation and a distinct appointment of a new party, the unlawful limb can be invalidated while leaving the appointment intact, especially where the latter has not been specifically challenged in pleadings and disturbing it would be unjust to the newly appointed party.

Remedial flexibility: In fundamental rights jurisdiction, the Court may craft just and equitable remedies that are not limited to simple declarations, including monetary compensation reflecting lost profits and structural orders such as directing the grant of a new dealership or, in the alternative, lump-sum compensation.

sc Gunaratne and Others v. Ceylon Petroleum Corporation and Others 315
GUNARATNE AND OTHERS
V.
CEYLON PETROLEUM CORPORATION AND OTHERS
SUPREME COURT.
FERNANDO, J.
DHEERARATNE, J. AND
ANANDACOOMARASWAMY, J.
S.C. APPLICATION NO. 99/96.
13 JUNE AND 05 JULY, 1996.
Fundamental Rights - Infringement of Article 12(1) of the Constitution- Dealership Agreement granting authority to sell, supply and distribute petroleum - Summary termination of Dealership Agreement - Should concept of executive or administrative action in relation to a contract be confined only to the "threshold stage"?
For many years before 1994 the 1st Petitioner had - as an individual - a Dealership Agreement together with the requisite authority under section 5E of the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation Act, No. 28 of 1961 as amended (by Act No. 5 of 1963) for running a filling station for the sale, supply and distribution of petroleum. The same filling station was taken over by the petitioners in partnership on a Dealership Agreement signed by the Petitioners on 23.3.94 and by 1st Respondent on 26.10.94 and the petitioners were granted authority with dealer discounts to sell, supply and distribute Lanka Two Star Petrol, Lanka Diesel and lubricants under section 5E of the Act. By letter dated 4.1.96 signed by the Marketing Manager of the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation (9th Respondent) the said Dealership Agreement was terminated. The authority was thus cancelled.
Clause 12B of the Agreement and section 5H (4) of the Act had provisions for the termination of the Agreement.
The Board of the Corporation had passed a resolution to terminate the dealership of the Petitioners and to grant the Dealership authority to one B. K. Sarath Wickramasiri (11th Respondent). The resolution was implemented without notice to the Petitioners. The resolution did not indicate any reason for the Board's decisions. However according to the letter of termination dated 4.1.96 the Board had considered the contents of five warning letters dated 23.2.81, 21.11.84, 19.5.86, 27.10.88 and 29.6.93 and had decided to terminate, with immediate effect the Petitioners' Agreement and authority, acting under Clause 12B and section 5H (4). The Corporation had a Marketing Manual setting out the procedure for the appointment of new dealers but this procedure was not followed. The 11th Respondent stated had made an application for a dealership in or about August 1995 and an interview had been held in the 9th Respondent's office and he was aware the Corporation's officials had made investigations into his application. There were however no pleadings or prayer in respect of the 11th Respondent's dealership.
The 9th Respondent had tendered a Board paper dated 8.12.95 wherein he mentioned the five warning letters and stated that although in the last warning, the dealer had been cautioned that any further act of misconduct would result in termination, considering the said serious lapses, he recommends to the Board of Directors to terminate the dealership.
Held:
(1) It is not only at the "threshold" stage (i.e.at or before the time the contract was entered into) that the Board's action could be regarded as executive or administrative action but also during the subsistence of the contract. The impugned resolution was administrative or executive action although it involved a contract and was in violation of Article 12(1).
(2) The Board was not entitled to cancel the authority or to terminate the Agreement without reasons. Further the Board was not made aware that four of the five warnings brought to its notice had occurred long before the current agreement and authority, and that the 2nd to 4th Petitioners were not involved in them; these should not have been taken into consideration. The fifth warning was in respect of an incident (defective pump) which had been dealt with, and was in any event insufficient to justify the termination, having regard to the Corporation's responsibility to supply and maintain equipment.
(3) The Agreement and the authority were intimately linked, and were in fact dealt with together and the first limb of the impugned resolution was therefore not severable. That part of the resolution was bad. However the second limb of the resolution (appointing 11th Respondent) was distinct and severable.
(4) There being no pleadings and prayer in respect of the appointment of the 11th Respondent it is not just and equitable to make any order affecting that appointment.
(5) The Petitioner's fundamental rights under Article 12(1) have been violated by the 1st to 8th Respondents by the termination of the agreement and the cancellation of the authority.
Cases referred to:
1. Roberts v. Ratnayake (1986) 2 Sri L.R. 36.
2. Wijenaike v. Air Lanka (1990) 1 Sri LR 293.
3. Dahanayake v. De Silva (1978-79-80) 1 Sri LR 47, 53-54.
APPLICATION for relief in respect of infringement of fundamental rights under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
Tilak Marapana P.C. with Nalin Ladduwahetty, Jayantha Fernando and Anuja Premaratne for Petitioners.
A.A. de Silva with Mahinda Ralapanawe for 1st to 9th Respondents, J.C. Weliamuna for the 11th Respondent.
Cur. adv.vult.
July 31, 1996.
FERNANDO, J.
The 1st Respondent, the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation, entered into a Dealership Agreement ("the Agreement") for the sale of petroleum products with the four Petitioners (who were carrying on business in partnership) in respect of the Kottawa Lanka Filling Station. That Agreement was signed by the Petitioners on 24.3.94 and by the 1st Respondent on 26.10.94. The Petitioners were granted authority to sell, supply and distribute petroleum under and in terms of section 5E of the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation Act, No. 28 of 1961, as amended. The Petitioners complain of the infringement of their fundamental rights under Article 12(1) by the 1st Respondent and the 2nd to 8th Respondents (the Chairman and Directors of the 1st Respondent) by reason of the summary termination of that Agreement, communicated by letter dated 4.1.96 signed by the Marketing Manager, the 9th Respondent, in consequence of which possession was taken on the same day; and the filling station was handed over to the 11th Respondent, the new dealer. There was no plea or prayer in respect of the cancellation of that authority.
For many years before 1994, the 1st Petitioner had - as an individual - a Dealership Agreement, together with the requisite authority under section 5E, in respect of the same filling station.
Clause 12B of the Agreement, and section 5H(4) of the Act, make the following provisions for the termination of the Agreement, and the statutory authority, as follows:
Clause 12B : If the Dealer does not in the opinion of the General Manager perform his duties and obligations as a Dealer of petroleum products of the Corporation faithfully, diligently and efficiently or if he defaults in complying with the terms, covenants and conditions of this Agreement or the terms and conditions under which commissions and allowances are payable to him referred to in paragraph 12 above, the Corporation shall be entitled to terminate agreement without any notice whatsoever. The Corporation shall also be entitled to terminate this Agreement after three months' notice in writing to the Dealer and the Dealer is entitled to terminate this Agreement after three months' notice in writing given to the Corporation. The three months' notice by the Dealer shall commence to run from the date on which the Corporation acknowledges the Dealer's written notice. Notwithstanding the above the Board of Directors may by a resolution passed at a meeting of the Board of Directors terminate this Agreement without notice and without assigning any reasons whatsoever.
Section 5H : "The following provisions shall be applicable in the case of the exercise of the power to grant a written authority conferred on the Minister, any authorized officer or the Board of Directors by any of the sections 5B, 5E, 5F and 5G: .......... ...............(4) The Minister, such officer or such Board may, in his or its absolute discretion, decide at any time to cancel such authority"
In an affidavit sworn on behalf of the 1st Respondent, the Deputy Marketing Manager produced the following Board resolution, which he said had been passed on 2.1.96: BOARD PAPER of 8.12.95 - TERMINATION OF DEALERSHIP OF KOTTAWA LANKA FILLING STATION - from Manager Marketing. Board decided: i) to terminate the dealership of Kottawa Lanka Filling Station at the Corporation Controlled Lanka Filling Station situated at Kottawa and cancel the authority granted to him under section 5H(4) of Ceylon Petroleum Corporation Act, No. 28 of 1961 as amended by Ceylon Petroleum Corporation (Amendment) Act, No. 5 of 1963 read with section 12(b) of the Dealership Agreement to sell, supply and distribute Lanka Two Star Petrol, Lanka Auto Diesel and Lubricants. ii) to appoint Mr. B.K. Sarath Wickramasiri of No. 201, Janarajaya Mawatha, Divulapitiya, Boralesgamuwa and grant him authority under section 5E of Ceylon Petroleum Corporation Act, No. 28 of 1961 as amended by Ceylon Petroleum Corporation (Amendment) Act, No. 5 of 1963, read with the terms and conditions set out in the Dealer Agreement to be signed hereinafter to sell, supply and distribute Lanka Two Star Petrol, Lanka Auto Diesel and Lubricants and grant him Corporation Controlled Dealer discounts." [...] I grant the Petitioners a declaration that their fundamental rights under Article 12(1) have been violated by the 1st to 8th Respondents by the termination of the Agreement and the cancellation of the authority, and award them compensation and costs in a sum of Rs 75,000. Had the Agreement been terminated with notice in terms of clause 12B, the petitioners would have made profits for a further period of three months, and that according to their uncontradicted assessment would have been Rs 500,000. I therefore further direct the 1st Respondent, at its option, either to grant the Petitioners (within six months from today) a dealership in respect of the same or another mutually acceptable filling station or to pay them compensation in a sum of Rs 500,000.
DHEERARATNE, J. - I agree.
ANANDACOOMARASWAMY, J. - I agree.
Relief granted.
source: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 99/96, decided on 31 July 1996

case_title: Gunaratne and Others v. Sri Lanka Telecom and Others (1992)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the new schemes of recruitment and promotion introduced by Sri Lanka Telecom, which granted preferential treatment to graduate clerks, violated the right to equality before the law under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, all non-graduate clerks employed by Sri Lanka Telecom, claimed that the newly adopted schemes of recruitment and promotion unfairly discriminated against them by granting preferential treatment to graduate clerks, regardless of whether their degrees were relevant to the duties of the higher posts. They argued that such classification was arbitrary, unreasonable, and violated their right to equality under Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the new schemes were formulated to enhance efficiency in the corporation and to address the grievances of under-employed graduates in public service. They argued that educational qualifications were a legitimate criterion for promotion and that the changes were necessary for the corporation’s evolving needs.
interpretation_summary: The Supreme Court held that while public corporations have the discretion to revise schemes of recruitment to meet service needs, such revisions must not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality. The preferential treatment accorded to graduate clerks in the new schemes was not based on an intelligible differentia that bore a rational connection to the objective of ensuring efficient service. The Court found the classification unreasonable because it gave advantage to graduate clerks (including those with irrelevant external degrees) while disregarding the legitimate expectations of experienced non-graduate clerks. The schemes were also found to prioritize social objectives—addressing underemployment among graduates—over the functional efficiency of the telecommunications service, which was an improper basis for internal promotion criteria.
outcome: The Court declared the preferential treatment given to graduate clerks under the new recruitment schemes (P11A and P11B) void for violating Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The Court ordered Sri Lanka Telecom to bear costs of Rs. 5,500 and allowed for the possibility of new, constitutionally compliant schemes to be introduced in the future.
principles_established: A recruitment or promotion scheme must be founded on an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the objective of the service.
Preferential treatment in employment cannot be justified by social or political considerations unrelated to the efficient functioning of the institution.
An inherently discriminatory scheme may be challenged immediately upon its adoption, without waiting for discriminatory implementation.
Educational qualifications must be relevant to the duties of the post to justify preferential treatment under Article 12(1).
full_text:
sc Gunaratne and Others v. Sri Lanka Telecom and Others
GUNARATNE AND OTHERS v. SRI LANKA TELECOM AND OTHERS
SUPREME COURT.
FERNANDO, J., KULATUNGA, J. AND WADUGODAPITIYA, J.
SC APPLICATION NO. 70/92.
15 JUNE, 1992.
Fundamental Rights - Scheme of Recruitment and Promotion - Favoured treatment to graduate clerks - Classification of graduate clerks - Discrimination - Article 12 (1) of the Constitution.
Upon the enactment of the Sri Lanka Telecommunications Act, No. 25 of 1991, the petitioners along with other officers who were in the service of the Telecommunications Department opted to become employees of the 1st respondent Corporation (Sri Lanka Telecom) under section 28 of the said Act. In terms of section 31 of the same Act they were entitled to terms and conditions not less favourable than those on which they had been employed in the Department of Telecommunications. On 03.01.1992 the Corporation adopted new schemes of recruitment to staff posts. The question for decision was whether the classification of the graduate clerks for preferential treatment in the new schemes was reasonable, the test of permissible classification being that it must be founded upon an intelligible differentia having a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved.
Held:
1. (a) If a scheme is prima facie non-discriminatory, it cannot be challenged in limine on the ground of possible discrimination in its application. In such a case, relief may be sought only upon the occurrence of discrimination.
(b) If however a scheme affecting promotions in an existing service is inherently discriminatory, as is alleged here, the right to relief accrues immediately upon the adoption of such scheme and prospective candidates for promotion under such scheme may apply for a declaration that such scheme is invalid on the ground that it constitutes an infringement or an imminent infringement of their rights under Article 12 (1).
2. (a) A variation of schemes of recruitment or preparation of a fresh scheme not violative of Article 12 (1) and dictated by the needs of the service, is permissible.
3. In the impugned schemes of recruitment:
(a) the express requirement of special ability and merit as a principle of promotion has been deleted.
(b) emphasis is placed on the requirement of a specific period of service with preferential treatment to graduate clerks.
(c) the new schemes whilst giving preferential treatment to graduate clerks, impose more stringent conditions on others by imposing a requisite period of service for promotion different from what is prescribed by the previous schemes.
(d) possession of a degree gives a clerk a preferential right to promotion without any consideration as to whether such degree is relevant to the duties of the higher post.
(e) the new schemes of recruitment have been prepared primarily with the object of alleviating the social grievances of under-employed graduates. In doing so the legitimate expectations of non-graduate clerks counting 20 to 30 years' of service have been disregarded.
(f) the new schemes are unreasonable because they are not based on criteria having a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved namely the efficient functioning of the Telecommunications Service.
(g) if it is desired to give preferential treatment to the graduate clerks in the interest of the service and for utilising their skills, the Corporation could do so on the basis of relevant qualifications, with reasonable notice to those affected and without prejudicing the legitimate expectations of clerks who are on the verge of promotion under the previous schemes.
APPLICATION for relief for infringement of fundamental rights.
R. K. W. Goonesekera with Peter Jayasekera, Suranjith Hewamanna and C. Swamadhipathy for the petitioners.
Asoka de Silva, D.S.G. with A Jinasena, S.C. for the respondents.
Cur. adv. vult.
August 24, 1992.
KULATUNGA, J.
The petitioners are Clerks, Class 1 in the Clerical Service of "Sri Lanka Telecom" (the 1st respondent) which is a public corporation established on 06.02.90 by an Order under s. 2 of the State Industrial Corporations Act, No. 49/1957. All of them had originally joined the Clerical Service of the former Posts and Telecommunications Department. Thereafter, when the Telecommunications Department was established as a separate Department, they continued in the Clerical Service of that Department, and were governed by the Minutes on the Telecommunications Clerical Service; and upon the enactment of the Sri Lanka Telecommunications Act, No. 25 of 1991 they, with other officers, opted to become employees of the 1st respondent Corporation under s. 28 of the said Act. In terms of s. 31 thereof, they were entitled to terms and conditions not less favourable than those on which they had been employed in the Department of Telecommunications.
The petitioners complain that the revised schemes for recruitment to Staff Grade posts in the Corporation afford more favoured treatment to graduate clerks. They were granted leave to proceed in respect of Article 12 (1) of the Constitution. In their application the petitioners also sought relief against a decision to appoint 6 graduate clerks to the Staff Grade, acting outside the scheme of recruitment. However, the learned Deputy Solicitor-General for the respondents informed us that the said decision will not be implemented. As such, the relief claimed by the petitioners is now limited to a declaration that the aforesaid revised schemes for recruitment are violative of their rights under Article 12 (1) and consequential reliefs. In addition to the Corporation, the petitioners have joined as parties to this application, the 2nd, the 3rd and the 4th respondents, being the Managing Director and the General Manager (Human Resources Development) of the Corporation, and the Secretary, Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications, respectively.
Originally, entry into the Clerical Service was through the Central Clerical Examination held by the Department of Examinations for candidates, the requisite educational qualification being the Senior School Certificate or the General Certificate of Education (Ordinary Level). From 1968, recruitment was by interview of eligible candidates. Under the Service Minute which continues to apply even after the establishment of the Corporation, the Clerical Service consists of Class II (with a cadre of 752) and Class I (with a cadre of 125). Initial recruitment is to segment B of Class II. Officers are promoted to segment A upon passing a qualifying examination after 4 years' of service. Their next promotion is to Class I on the basis of seniority and merit. A clerk in Class I is eligible upon selection by examination and interview to be appointed to the post of Examiner of Accounts which post forms an integral part of the Clerical Service. The cadre of Class I Clerks and Examiners of Accounts is 125.
Staff Posts in the Telecommunication Service and the cadre in each grade consist of:
(a) Administrative Assistant (07)
(b) Assistant Administrative Secretary/Assistant Superintendent (Commercial) being posts carrying the same salary scale, (24 and 15 respectively)
(c) Administrative Secretary (04)
(d) Commercial Superintendent (01)
(e) Senior Administrative Secretary (01)
Until 1988, vacancies in the post of Administrative Assistant were filled by promoting Class I Clerks/Examiners of Accounts on the basis of seniority and merit. The promotion of Administrative Assistants to the post of Assistant Administrative Secretary/Assistant Superintendent (Commercial) was also on the basis of seniority and merit.
On 06.06.88 a new scheme of recruitment to the post of Assistant Administrative Secretary/Assistant Superintendent (Commercial) was adopted. Under the said scheme the following officers are eligible for promotion: (i) Administrative Assistants, (ii) Class I Clerks with 6 years' service, (iii) Examiners of Accounts with 6 years' combined service as Examiners and Class I Clerks. Appointments are made after interview by a Selection Board, preference being given to merit over seniority.
On 01.12.88 a scheme of recruitment to the next higher staff grade viz. Administrative Secretary was adopted in terms of which an officer with 3 years' service as Assistant Administrative Secretary/Assistant Superintendent (Commercial) is eligible for promotion to that grade on the basis of seniority and merit. The selection for promotion is after interview by a Selection Board.
The above schemes of recruitment appear to have been generally acceptable to the majority of the officers in the Telecommunications Department. However, the graduate clerks were not satisfied with their promotional prospects under the said schemes. Acting on their representations the 5th respondent had (in June, 1990) directed the Department to prepare draft amendments to the schemes of recruitment providing for preferential treatment to graduate clerks in the matter of promotion to staff posts. This was challenged in SC Application No. 25/90 by the Telecommunication Clerical Service Union and 3 non-graduate clerks. The said application was withdrawn in November 1990 in view of the averments in the affidavit of the 5th respondent which indicated that the impugned proposals for amendments to the schemes of recruitment will not be implemented, particularly in view of the impending transfer of Telecommunication Services to the Corporation.
On 03.01.90 the Corporation adopted the following new schemes of recruitment to staff posts:
Administrative Assistant: Class I Clerks with 6 years' service and Examiners of Accounts with 6 years' combined service as Examiner and Class I Clerk are eligible for promotion. Where such officer is a graduate, only 2 years' service is required.
Assistant Administrative Secretary/Assistant Commercial Superintendent: Administrative Assistants with 1 year's service or 8 years' combined service as Administrative Assistant and Class I Clerk; Class I Clerks with 8 years' service and Examiners of Accounts with 8 years' combined service. Where any such officer is a graduate, only 4 years' service is required.
Administrative Secretary: Assistant Administrative Secretaries/Assistant Commercial Superintendents with 3 years' combined service in the said grade and as Administrative Assistants are eligible for promotion. Appointment to each of the above grades will be by promotion of eligible officers on the recommendation of a Selection Board, after an interview.
The petitioners state that the preferential treatment sought to be given to graduate clerks has no rational basis and hence amounts to discrimination violative of Article 12 (1) of the Constitution. The 2nd respondent states that the object of the revised schemes is to provide for a better and more reasonable method of promotion and that the proposed new criteria for promotion are based \"mainly on the efficiency of the officers to be promoted\". He adds that in preparing these schemes the grievances of under-employed graduates in the public service were also taken into consideration.
source: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, SC Application No. 70/92, decided on 24 August 1992

case_title: Jayanetti v. The Land Reform Commission and Others (1984)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the Land Reform Commission’s decision to alienate land to an ineligible applicant while rejecting the petitioner’s application constituted unequal treatment and a violation of the fundamental right to equality under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that the Land Reform Commission unfairly rejected his application to purchase 50 acres of Mount Pearl Estate while approving the same land for Mrs. Dassanayake, a public corporation employee who was legally disqualified under section 23 of the Land Reform Law. He claimed this amounted to discriminatory and arbitrary administrative action in violation of Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the Minister and the Land Reform Commission acted lawfully within the framework of the Land Reform Law, that the petitioner’s application lacked merit, and that any procedural irregularities did not amount to a violation of fundamental rights. They further argued that the petition was out of time and that additional parties could not be added beyond the statutory limit under Rule 65(1)(b) of the Supreme Court Rules.
interpretation_summary: The Court held that the Land Reform Commission was an instrumentality of the State and that its acts constituted ‘executive or administrative action’ under Article 126. The failure to follow mandatory legal requirements—including Gazette publication under section 26, adherence to eligibility criteria under section 23, and fair consideration of the petitioner’s application—amounted to unequal treatment. The Court ruled that the preferential alienation of land to a disqualified person (a State Corporation employee) while rejecting the petitioner’s valid application violated Article 12(1). The Court also clarified that the two-month time limit for fundamental rights applications is directory, not mandatory, and that necessary parties may be added to ensure a fair hearing. Further, it affirmed that ‘law’ in Article 12(1) includes both legislative and administrative action, and that Article 126 provides the sole and expeditious remedy for fundamental rights violations.
outcome: The Court declared that the alienation of the land to Mrs. Dassanayake was null and void for violating the petitioner’s right to equality under Article 12(1). It held that the transfer deed and related proceedings were invalid and directed the Land Reform Commission to take appropriate lawful action regarding the land. No costs were awarded.
principles_established: The Land Reform Commission is an agency or instrumentality of the State, and its actions constitute executive or administrative action under Article 126.
Article 12(1) protects against unequal treatment arising from both legislative and administrative acts.
Procedural rules are subordinate to constitutional guarantees; justice requires flexibility in adding parties and managing timelines.
The statutory requirement for Gazette publication of alienations is mandatory to ensure fairness and equality.
Preferential or politically influenced treatment in administrative decisions violates the principle of equality before the law.
precedents_cited: K.K. Kochunni v. State of Madras (AIR 1955 SC 725)
